You were asked about commanders at any level and if they were prosecuted for crimes perpetrated against Kosovo Albanians, and your answer was: "As far as I can remember, based on all the surveys, I think there must have been around 10 such officers, and I'm talking about officers now." Do you stand by that figure, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, during your testimony on direct, we heard a lot of information, detailed information, about the activities of the KLA right down to meetings that they were holding in another country in Switzerland. And you had information about that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, how is it that you can know about a meeting of the KLA in Switzerland but you did not hear of an entire valley of people being expelled and 300 people being killed right in Djakovica? How is that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When analysing Albanian separatism and terrorism, we didn't analyse it just in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija because they were linked to the extreme Albanian immigration residing in Switzerland and Germany first and foremost. We planted our people into those environments, and they provided intelligence to us. This is something that all intelligence and counter-intelligence services nowadays do. So we are no different from them. Your question is how come. And that was our routine, permanent job. And then you asked how come we were able to gather such information and on the other hand were unable to collect plain information. The answer is that we did not investigate some hot spot. We did have information that a large group of civilians was on its way to Djakovica and now you are asking me how come we didn't learn that those civilians were treated inhumanely. I'm telling you that there was no way we could obtain such information because we did not have our people among those civilians. We had no positions among them. Even (redacted), who was an agent of the security service, didn't tell us that. K73, the protected witness, didn't tell us this either. And their constitutional obligation, both of them, was such that they as soldiers of the army of the Yugoslavia whenever they learned that somebody was committing a crime were duty-bound to report it to relevant authorities. So the question is how come they did not inform Captain Perovic, Colonel Dosan, or myself of those events or anybody at the forward command post? Wasn't that logical for them to inform any army member of what they had seen, heard, or observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: First, just as an administrative matter, maybe we can deal with this at the end of the session, but I will probably need to close some portions of that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm, at the moment, having a name redacted, page 49, line 16 and 17. If there's more, raise it when you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, I don't want to get too much into a debate about this. For your information, the information of (redacted) was that Captain Perovic was well aware of this. But, sir, let's go back to your knowledge. Now, it's my understanding, from what you've said, your sources that report to you about crimes within the VJ are all within the VJ, correct? They are your security officers, commanders, the officers themselves, operatives; they're within the VJ. Is that correct? That's what triggers the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sources of information of the security service, [indiscernible], and that is prescribed for all services including the military security service. One of our services were people, persons, all the members of the army. There was one source. In addition to that, we had special people who had a special cooperative relationship with the security service. The third type of sources were commanders who were at the top of the chain of command. The following source were -- was the media and electronic media. So, as I have said to you, there were numerous sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, I think we've been through this a lot. It appears to me that the answer to that question, the question that I just asked you, if we are looking at all the sources you just named, you named members of the army; special people with a cooperative relationship, which I believe are also within the army, if I've understood your testimony correctly; commanders; and I think you would say the security organs below. Those are the primary people who report to you every day; correct? That's your primary source of information of what's going on with regard to VJ crimes or those security organs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, let me ask you this: In the case of systematic, planned activity that is criminal such as expelling civilians, are you not, in effect, relying on the army to report on itself?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday or the day before, I said that in addition to our agents, our collaborators in the army, we also had our collaborators out in the field. The protected witness, whose name I'm not going to mention, who does not have a pseudonym that starts with a K, is our person from that area. And he did not report anything to anyone. Had we had some of our people, some of our agents within that group of people that had formed a refugee column, I'm sure that he would have informed us of that, but we didn't. We had our people elsewhere in the territory. And in that group we did not have a person who could have informed us of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, I believe the testimony from that witness that we have is that Captain Perovic who reported to you daily was well aware of the situation. So either for some reason he didn't tell you, or he did and you're not telling us everything you know today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never told me that, and I inquired several times. And his statement was quite different from the statement of the gentleman that you have mentioned. His statement was that he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Sir, let's move on to another topic now. You said that in 1998 you did not attend meetings of the Joint Command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend the meetings where co-ordination and concerted action were discussed, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. You'd heard about them, but you yourself did not attend?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of such meetings, but I never attended them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, it was from Milan Djakovic that you got this information about the Joint Command, or that you heard of it, I'm sorry, you heard of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. And I believe you said in your testimony here that you gave reports on the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija to Djakovic and that it's your understanding that he then took those to the Joint Command meetings; is that a fair summary of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an obligation vis-à-vis the chief of the department who planned operations, and that was Colonel Milan Djakovic, to forward all information to him concerning terrorists. He, in turn, exchanged that information in various meetings where planning and co-ordination were the topics of the day with the MUP staff in Pristina. And occasionally he would issue a report, sort of a news bulletin, containing that information. And that was quite useful for me in making my own assessment of the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at -- this was government's -- it's now an exhibit, but I have -- it's Prosecution 65 ter 02945, and the Exhibit number is now 1543. If we could just have that on the screen. And if we could, in that, go to page 10 in the English, and in the B/C/S page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And in B/C/S the relevant portion is that box number 2, if we look at it in English, this is from the Pristina Corps Command Security Sector dated November 11, 1998. And it appears to be an intelligence report, and it states at the top: "To the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." Is this an example of the type of information that you would pass to Djakovic that he would then take to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not an example. This refers to the 11th of November, 1998. On one or two occasions, and perhaps it was just this single case I -- if Colonel Djakovic was in hurry to get to the meeting with the MUP staff, the co-ordination meeting, then he would tell me to type up the information that I acquired in the preceding seven days. The regular routine was for me to type up or convey verbally to Djakovic whatever information I had for him to take to this meeting where co-ordination and concerted action were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, sometimes you just gave him the information that he would pass on, but there were some occasions where you wrote up something like this? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 99 per cent of the cases, I would forward the typed-up information to the chief of the operations department, Colonel Djakovic. In this case and perhaps some additional two or three cases, when he was in a hurry, I would ask him how to draft the document, and he would tell me, Address it to the Joint Command and bring it downstairs to my office and I would take it with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, in Milutinovic you said you may have written multiple reports such as this. Does that sound right to you now?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. This was very seldom for this to be in writing. Normally it would just be typed up on a plain piece of paper because Djakovic and I were from the same command, and I would just hand it to him and would he compare it to the information coming in from the SUP and compile his own information and then publish it in the bulletin which came out -- which was published sometime from June 1998 to late November 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of David Gajic from the state security department attending the Joint Command meetings in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, David Gajic was chief of the state security department for the territory of the entire Kosovo. Based on the information I received from Djakovic and on the information I received from Colonel Slobodan Djindjic who was deputy security chief of the 3rd Army, and I told you yesterday that occasionally he would visit the Pristina Corps security department, and I think that on two occasions he also attended these meetings of co-ordination and concerted action. I learned that Gajic would also occasionally attend these meetings or somebody else from his state security department.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And did you know of other people who attended the meetings? Did you know if Sainovic attended the meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My source of information was Djakovic or, on two or three occasions, it was Djindjic as I have told you. And they told me that Nikolai Sainovic occasionally attended those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Now, after the Joint Command meetings, would Djakovic bring new information back that had been reported by the state security? Would you be informed of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings of co-ordination and concerted action between the Pristina Corps and the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija were not held on a regular basis. Based on what I know, they were held in the aftermath [as interpreted] of some anti-terrorist organisation. But when Djakovic or Tesovic or somebody else from the operations department pursuant to an agreement reached by Pavkovic or somebody else about exchanging information, in those situations, I would send to Djakovic on a daily basis our information and somebody would bring it from the MUP or he would go to the MUP to get that information, and then, almost daily, a bulletin would be published covering the entire situation in Kosovo, including attacks on civilian population, crimes committed by terrorists, security, communication, what were the plans of the army units and what they had done. This was just a snap-shot of the security situation, and it was published in the form of a bulletin, and it was known as the Report of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And did that include information from the state security service, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that bulletin, most of the information was from the area of intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that answers my question. I just want to know if it included information from state security. Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at this point in 1998 you were still sending intelligence telegrams to both the 3rd Army and the General Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the beginning of the NATO aggression, yes, both the 3rd Army and the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And in 1998 the chief of the security administration in the General Staff was General Dimitrijevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Colonel-General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, did -- I believe you said that a Radojko Stefanovic took over for Djakovic around January of 1999 in your Milutinovic testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, January 1999. Late January/early February. But I'd leave it at January. It's a very small discrepancy, if anything; I'm not sure I can be perfectly accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. And in your Milutinovic testimony at 20050, you said that Stefanovic continued to provide with you information discussed at the Joint Command meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was providing me with information about this bulletin that I mentioned called the "Report of the Joint Command." During 1999, there were no co-ordination and concerted action meetings on account of NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Let me just read the exact testimony so we make sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being told that - this is page 55, line 9 - it says that the co-ordination meetings were held after, in the aftermath of anti-terrorist operations. And I do believe that the answer referred to before anti-terrorist operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You wish to clarify that, Ms. Petersen?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Which line was it specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 55, line 9. He talks about the time these co-ordination meetings were held.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, in speaking about the Joint Command meetings at this point in the transcript it says: "The meetings of co-ordination and concerted action between the Pristina Corps and the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija were not held on a regular basis. Based on what I know, they were held in the aftermath of some anti-terrorist organisation." Was that your answer or is there something that you would like to correct there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I talked about the co-ordination and concerted action meetings; Pavkovic and Djakovic decided to term those Joint Command meetings. I said those weren't held on a regular basis, rather, only whenever an anti-terrorist operation was being planned or was in the making.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And that was your understanding from Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Now, just to be clear, the testimony I was just putting to you from Milutinovic on page 20050, the question was: "Who informed you about the information shared by the state security at these meetings?" Your answer was: "The chief of the operative department of the Pristina Corps Command General Djakovic put that to me and then Radojko Stefanovic." And you were asked who was Radojko Stefanovic, and you said: "Colonel Radojko Stefanovic was from the beginning of 1999, well, he replaced Colonel Djakovic as chief of the department for operative affairs of the Pristina Corps Command." So that's the question to you. Did you continue to get information from Colonel Stefanovic when he took over in 1999 about information from state security at these Joint Command meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think what can be -- I don't see what can be disputed about that. I said that during the NATO air-strikes, there was always from the MUP or someone from army who would go get the information that related to intelligence and security related matters, all the way up until April when all this information ceased. But this information was previously used to draft the so-called report of the Joint Command or an information bulletin, whatever you prefer to call it. What I said about concerted action and the exchange of information between the Pristina Corps and the MUP staff in terms of planning and carrying out anti-terrorist operations, there was none in 1999. It was physically impossible, given the fact that both the Pristina Corps Command and the staff were located dispersively, i.e., they were at several different locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand that. It was physically impossible to have a Joint Command meeting; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was physically impossible. And because of the general situation, we were trying to set up a defence operation. We were expected to be attacked by an enemy landing. The focus during the NATO aggression was on preparing our defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, how was it physically impossible? Who couldn't meet?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessment was right after the beginning of the NATO aggression that there would be no need anymore for these co-ordination and concerted action meetings, that being the reason those were not held throughout 1999. Nevertheless, the bulletin continued to be produced right up through mid-April. Someone, for example, knows where the MUP staff is located, they get the information that the state security service gave to the MUP, then I go down a flight of stairs to see an operative officer to get my information. This is then typewritten in the Pristina Corps, it's filed away, and a copy of the bulletin is served on the MUP staff while another copy is forwarded to the Pristina Corps Command. So there were times when those --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So these reports were still being issued by the Joint Command during this time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the reports were being produced by the Pristina Corps Command, and they weren't just being sent to the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps by road, rather, they were sometimes also sent to some state bodies dealing with negotiations with Rugova and other Albanian leaders, and as far as I remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If -- let's try to keep the answers related to the questions so that we can move through this a little more quickly, sir. You are saying that these came from the Pristina Corps Command. While they may have been drafted there, these were -- these said "Joint Command," did they not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer directly. The co-ordination and concerted action meetings held by Pavkovic and Djakovic in 1998 and termed by them Joint Command meetings, co-ordination and concerted action with the MUP on the eve of any anti-terrorist operation, those were never held during the NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: My question for you is whether these reports said "Joint Command." That is the question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up until April. Most of the documents were produced by the Joint Command in relation to each operation that was launched. Nevertheless, Colonel Radojko Stefanovic took over from Djakovic and that was when what he found when he took over. It was by inertia that he continued to write the same kind of thing. He had just become an operative and then Djakovic, who continued by inertia, continued to use this term, Joint Command. Nevertheless, in practical terms, these co-ordination and concerted action meetings, be it in the MUP or in the army, were no longer held.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, do I take it your testimony is that the words "Joint Command" on these reports coming out were just a holdover? That was just on the form? It had no more meaning than that. Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I will endeavour to clarify. The Joint Command is a term somewhat awkwardly agreed on by Pavkovic and Djakovic. It was mostly used in 1998 during the anti-terrorist operations and continued to be used up through late November when the OSCE Mission arrived and established control in Kosovo and in that period of time there were no more anti-terrorist operations to speak of. To all practical intents. These were co-ordination and concerted action meetings. This Joint Command, did it exist in the sense that you're asking? If it had existed, it should have been -- it's establishment should have been ordered by someone, Set up such and such a Joint Command. It would have needed to have an establishment and structure. The Joint Command shall comprise the following ... and then on like that. Next thing, this Joint Command would need to have a place in the chain of command so that everyone knew who was subordinated to it and who were its superiors. It should have been made very specific what their tasks and obligations were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, my --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you is this: You have stated there were these reports or bulletins coming out that said Joint Command up until April 1999. Are you saying that although they say Joint Command, that wasn't really who they were from? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain two different terms to you here. The document's entitled "Joint Command;" the other is a document entitled "The Report of the Joint Command." These are two different things. Now please ask me what exactly you expect me to explain about these two things.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, first, we can agree that multiple documents, orders, and reports came out in 1999 saying they were from the Joint Command; is that correct? We can agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were designated as the Joint Command, but they did not issue from the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: But they said they were from the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they just said the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Why don't we --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Why don't we look at one of these documents to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at P973. Actually, why don't we go a little bit later. If we could look at P1328.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And we see this is dated 15th April, 1999. At the top it says it's from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, and it gives an order to break up and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the Rugovo sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And if we could look at the last page in both documents. Scrolling up a little bit, I guess it's the second to the last in English. Down at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: It says: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command all forces from the Pristina sector during the conduct of combat operations." Now, sir, we won't go through all of these here, but there are numerous of these orders coming from the Joint Command in evidence in this case, and most of them have some type of statement like that at the bottom also in some form. If you could just tell us, this appears very clearly to be an order from a Joint Command. Are you telling us that in 1999 this did not exist; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not exist in 1999. This is not an order by the Joint Command. This is an order by the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, we have heard evidence in this case, we have gone through documents and heard evidence that it is important that a particular stamp be in a particular corner and a particular received stamp be in a particular place and that if those things aren't there, then the document is not authentic. You are telling us that a document can say it is from something, it can be from an origin that doesn't even exist, and that's okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll simplify. If you can bring back page 1 and then I'll explain the whole document to you by your Chamber's leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, let's try to keep it focused on the question which is your contention that the Joint Command does not -- is a body that does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document, your question for me is to comment on this document, right? Do you want me to explain why --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: My question for you is, with the title that it's coming from a Joint Command and a statement at the end about the Joint Command commanding, how can you say that this body does not exist? That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that. Firstly, if you look at the filing number for this document, it's from the Pristina Corps Command. Secondly, all these documents were written at the Pristina Corps Command. Thirdly, throughout this document, all you see are assignments for the units of the Pristina Corps. Had there been such a command as the one you call the Joint Command, then the document wouldn't read such and such a unit of the Pristina Corps and such and such an assignment. It would have been joint security forces, meaning the MUP and the army are to carry out such and such assignments. Why does the title say the Joint Command and why does the signature say the Joint Command? It was based on agreement. This was a signal to subordinate commanders, specifically the commander caring out these particular operation, that these activities had been co-ordinated and agreed upon between the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps Command. The commander knew when he received an order like this that the same order would be received by the commander who in this situation is co-ordinating this on the MUP side. What this means is they have to meet up, they have to set out everything in great detail as to how they would be implementing this operation. The Joint Command here is a signal to the commander of the appropriate unit, meaning that these activities were agreed, co-ordination and concerted action between the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps Command. That's what it means. Most of the documents bear this marking.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So, sir, you're explaining that this is a mechanism for co-ordinated action between the MUP and the VJ, correct, which was still very necessary during the NATO bombing period in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary during 1999. It was by pure inertia. It was something that was in the computer of the Pristina Corps. It was Stefanovic and all those operatives who were there. It was by pure inertia they continue to type up orders using this phrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I need you to listen to the specific question I'm asking you. I ask you if co-ordinated action, co-ordination, between the VJ and the MUP was still important in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It always was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And this is a mechanism for achieving that; these orders of the Joint Command co-ordinate that action between the VJ and the MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: No, no. I just need -- if you disagree with me, then say so. If that is accurate. I believe that's what you just said, I'm trying to repeat what you said accurately. Is that right or not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Throughout 1998, there were meetings, co-ordination and concerted action meetings, between the MUP and the army that were held. In 1999, during NATO aggression, no meetings were held. This clerk from the Pristina Corps would go to see an operative. Most frequently, I think it was Colonel Adamovic at the MUP staff. And then they would deal with this together. The two of them would do the co-ordination bit; he would then go back and type up a document like this for use by subordinate units. And this was hint to them that this was something that had been agreed with the MUP staff in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that the co-ordination between the VJ and the MUP amounted to a clerk from the Pristina Corps going to see an operative; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of the operations department would normally, or his clerk, would normally meet with the chief of the operations department in the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry I thought you said an operative.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I have a different topic to go on at this point. I notice we are about five minutes from the break. It would be a good point to break, if you don't mind breaking a little early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you some questions about the 1st June, 1999, meeting. This meeting was over ten years ago; correct? Eight years before you testified in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And you yourself did not take notes at this meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: How many people were at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, let's go through who you've said was there: General Pavkovic, one; Lazarevic, correct, two; Sainovic, correct; Andjelkovic, correct; Mico Valotic [phoen], correct; Kovacevic, correct; yourself; and Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So eight. Now, was there possibly another MUP representative there? Oh, I'm sorry, we forgot to say Lukic, so nine. In addition to that, was there possibly another MUP representative there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, when you testified in Milutinovic at page 19801, you said: "Possibly there was another MUP representative." In the last two years, has your memory gotten better about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I -- I don't know, maybe there was a clerk from the MUP staff there as well. But as for these nine, I'm certain; for the rest, I'm not. But I think that it is more likely that my answer is no, that there were just nine of them, as far as I could remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So it's possible there was a clerk for the MUP, and I think you said "for the rest, I'm not sure." Is it possible that were other people at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, you said two years ago that there might have been another representative from the MUP; you're telling us you now you're not sure. It sounds like you are not actually positive about the attendees at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that these nine were there certainly. And in saying so, I'm conscious of the fact that I'm not certain whether General Lukic sat on his own or there was somebody there sitting next to him. If there was an additional person, then it was one of his clerks. However, it is much more likely that there was nobody else there apart from these nine persons. But please do not forget that it's been 11 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. So nine, maybe ten. All right. This was a short meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very short. Not longer than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You didn't know about it beforehand, before you were invited?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So it's fair to say you were sort of invited at the last minute to go to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, one of the senior officers from the information centre gave me a message from the corps commander that I should come to this meeting, and that General Pavkovic would be there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And that was on the day of the meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the day of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you didn't have to do any special preparation for this meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because corps commander could call me frequently, and usually his requests vis-à-vis me were always identical, he needed to know about security issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, other than Pavkovic who invited you, I believe you said you didn't know who was going to be there until you arrived and saw them; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know who would be there. I didn't know that until I entered the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Sir, you were asked several questions about the testimony of General Vasiljevic, and I'd just like to go through a few of these things. At page 11788 of the transcript, you were asked: "I'd like to show you portions of General Vasiljevic's testimony before this Tribunal." Going on to the next page. In the transcript he said that he called General Pavkovic and told him that he had arrived in Pristina. Pavkovic wanted to see him and invited him to the Pristina Corps Command. Does this correspond to what you know? And you answered: "I have no knowledge of General Pavkovic speaking to Mr. Vasiljevic, but I explained in detail the only meeting which I attended when I saw Pavkovic." Now, I'd like to correct something here. In reality, General Vasiljevic's testimony was this, and I'd like you to comment on this. He says he arrived in Pristina on June 1st, and on page 5691 of the transcript he says: "The evening of 1st of June we were briefed on the situation by the head of the security service of the Pristina Corps Colonel Momir Stojanovic. However, military regulations order us and it's a matter of ethics that when ever somebody comes to a command post, the commander should be informed of that. Colonel Stojanovic phoned General Pavkovic telling him that I arrived in Pristina." Does this accord with your memory? Could it have happened that way?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, did I not call Colonel Pavkovic on the phone. The premises where the staff of the security organ was housed contained several telephones and several rooms, so I don't know whether somebody informed Pavkovic. I couldn't call Pavkovic myself because he was way high up. I could have talked to Lazarevic, but I didn't. It is possible that Vasiljevic, while staying in those premises, talked to Pavkovic on the phone, telling him that he was in the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps. However, this did not take place in my presence. I'm not aware of him talking to Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Next at your testimony the other day, on page 11789, the question was: "General Vasiljevic further states that the two of you went to the command of the Pristina Corps and that General Pavkovic said, Stay here, there will be a Joint Command meeting followed by a dinner. Does this tally with what you know?" And you said: "Definitely not. Since General Vasiljevic was sitting next to me, I didn't notice" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: "... I didn't notice him speaking to anyone after the meeting. I don't even know whether, under such circumstances, any dinner was planned and whether it would have been possible." Now, in the Milutinovic trial, the Court heard from Andjelkovic, who you recall was at this meeting, and he stated - this is an exhibit in this case, it's P1541, page 67 - he said that he did have a dinner at this meeting. Is it possible that you're just mistaken and that some people were invited to a dinner and you were not necessarily aware of it? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First you quoted my previous statement in the Milutinovic trial; you said some things that I didn't actually say back then, that I went to the Pristina Corps Command. The place that I went to was the information centre of the Pristina Corps Command, not the Pristina Corps Command itself, and that was the room that the meeting was held in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I think -- I think we have a little misunderstanding. What I just read from -- to you was from this case, and it was a question about -- well, let me just re-read it because I think we have a misunderstanding about what I am asking you. This was a question put to you in this case. General Vasiljevic further states that the two of you went to the command of the Pristina Corps and that General Pavkovic said: "Stay here, there will be a Joint Command meeting followed by a dinner. Does this tally with what you know?" And you answered: "Definitely not. Since General Vasiljevic was sitting next to me, I didn't notice him speaking to anyone after the meeting. I don't even know whether under such circumstances any dinner was planned and whether it would have been possible." So that was the testimony here. My question for you was: In light of testimony by Mr. Andjelkovic in the Milutinovic case, that he did have dinner with this meeting; is it possible that you're mistaken in your claim that it wasn't even possible to have a dinner? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've read a number of things that I have stated. It's all accurate. I stand by it. I wasn't wrong. The evening that the meeting was concluded, General Vasiljevic left with me and went back. There was no talk of any dinner or anything like that. Now, about the seven days that he spent in Kosovo and Metohija, did he attend dinner with someone or not? I really don't know. All I can tell you about is the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, first, sir, the testimony of Mr. Vasiljevic is that he was invited to a dinner but did not stay and left with you. So just to be clear about that. But let me understand your testimony here. Are you telling us that even though Mr. Andjelkovic says he attending a dinner, that's impossible, no dinner happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that we did not attend any sort of dinner after that meeting. I wasn't invited. Vasiljevic was seated right next to me. And we went back to where we came from, the deployment area of the security section of the Pristina Corps. That is the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And I'm asking you: Is it possible that General Vasiljevic was invited to this dinner and you were not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. That evening, after that meeting, no, it was impossible, because he want back with me to the deployment sector of the security section. I'm sure that he did not attend any dinner that particular evening because he was with us security officers looking into our problems. Was there perhaps a different day, because he was in Kosovo from the 1st to the 7th, and then perhaps on that other day he attended dinner somewhere, well, that's certainly a possibility. I don't have any information indicating that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I clarified for you that General Vasiljevic said he was invited to a dinner but did not stay and left with you. My question is: Is it possible that he was invited to a dinner and you are not aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that he was invited. Nevertheless, we left right after the meeting. When was it that he could have been invited? Maybe someone whispered an invitation into his ear, Stay for dinner, which I can hardly be expected to know or have noticed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. Now, the next thing I'd like to look at is still on the page of your testimony 11789, your testimony in this case. You were asked: Next General Vasiljevic states that the place where you were was something like an operations room with maps on walls and lots of officers, does this correspond to the location you remember as the place of the meeting?" And you answered: "No, the operations room is usually next to the office of the corps commander. The corps commander was deployed in several locations around Pristina, changing locations from time to time, and the operations organ was always next to the commander because that person was in charge of suggesting what combat operations would be undertaken." And then I believe you said that it was in fact the information centre where you were. Now, I understand that you say you were in the information centre, General Vasiljevic believed he was in the operation centre. My question for you is this, sir: There's no dispute that the two of you were at the same meeting together; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were at the same meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you testified in the Milutinovic trial; correct? We've spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: When you testified in that trial, as you sit here today, can you tell us which people in the courtroom took notes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Stamp who was examining me. I don't know who was taking notes in the courtroom. The lawyer was Mr. Bakrac, but I don't know who was taking notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, no one can blame you for that, right, because that's not normally something that we notice and commit to memory, will you agree? Who's taking notes, who's not taking notes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. In Milutinovic, you were asked at transcript page 19805. "That 10 to 15-minute meeting that you spoke about, did anybody keep notes? Did anybody make a record?" And you answered: "Let me repeat. Nobody kept minutes or a record. Nobody even took notes." Now, sir, is it your testimony that for this meeting almost 11 years ago, you remember that no one in the room even took notes? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam Prosecutor, I misunderstood. You asked me at the Milutinovic trial in the courtroom, that was my understanding of your question, who was examining me and who was taking notes. And now you're asking me about a specific meeting. Was anyone taking notes? No one was taking notes at that meeting because it was extremely brief and extremely unpleasant. No one was taking notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So your testimony to us is that you recall, for all of those people in the room, you remember and have committed to memory for 11 years who was taking notes or that no one was taking notes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully. There were nine of us there, and we were all in that room roughly the same size as this room. We were all close together. There was no need after all. This was a meeting where information was to be exchanged. Given the nature of the information, I don't know what there was to take down. Some action, some assignment. I remember clearly and with a great degree of certainty that no one there was taking notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, when information is exchanged, some people may jot that information down on a piece of paper; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some people jot it down later on after the meeting. Regardless of that, does the information tally with what was actually said? Well, that's a different issue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm asking you about your memory of a meeting almost 11 years ago where you're telling this Court that you know, you remember today, that no one took notes at that meeting. That's what I'm asking you about. So, sir, when Mr. Sainovic was speak to you, he was delivering information about political negotiations; right? When he was speaking to you, were you looking around the room to see if anyone -- instead of looking at him, were you looking around the room to see if anyone was writing anything down?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, no one had a note pad in front of them to begin with. They should probably -- wouldn't have written this down on the desk in front of them. This was the most difficult meeting that I ever attended. It was an extremely unpleasant meeting because the meeting concerned the decision for me to leave my native area. I did notice one thing, and I'll tell you who commented on what. What I noticed is that no one had a note pad or a notebook open in front of them to jot things down.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So while you were learning this difficult information, you took the time and effort to look around and note whether anyone was writing in a notebook and remember that; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm entirely certain. I had sufficient presence of mind to notice that. It's a very small room, a relatively small room, nine people sitting there, I would have noticed someone writing things down. It wouldn't have been that difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, how about this additional MUP representative who may or may not have even been there, do you remember if he was or wasn't taking notes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My certainty is not 90 per cent, but it's quite high. I'm quite certain, though, that only General Lukic, the commander of the MUP staff was there and no one else from their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, you, I believe, have stated that this was not a meeting of the Joint Command; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've established that you didn't have advanced knowledge of this meeting; you were invited to it the day of it; it was a 15-minute meeting that you attended and then left. Correct? All those things are true? And we've also established that in 1998 when the Joint Command --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: We've established in 1998, when you agree that the Joint Command was meeting, you yourself did not attend any of those meetings; correct? In 1998.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So you have no firsthand knowledge of those meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So, sir, you have no firsthand basis for saying whether this was or was not a meeting of the Joint Command, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I say that this was a Joint Command meeting if it had no planning purpose or anything like that? General Pavkovic, who as the first to address those assembled, told us that Mr. Sainovic had arrived and that he wanted to inform us on the progress of the negotiations, the talks between Mr. Milosevic and the two mediators at the final stage -- while it was in progress, I wasn't sure about the final stage. So this was the information shared with us by Mr. Pavkovic as he was opening that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: But, sir, you are stating an opinion that you know this was not a meeting of the Joint Command, and I'm asking you how you have any firsthand basis for knowing that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about any firsthand basis. I know about the co-ordination and concerted action meetings, at least based on what Djakovic told me or what Djindjic told me, the two times he attended those. There were always different people attending. You hardly ever had the same people attending these meetings. The only people who were always the same group were those from the MUP staff and those from the Pristina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree that you have no firsthand knowledge of what a Joint Command meeting is or is not like; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I categorically claim that that was no Joint Command meeting. If you allow, the people present at that meeting were the most responsible people and the people with the highest degree of responsibility to do with the withdrawal of the JNA from Kosovo: The chief of the security service, the chief of the military security service, the state security service, the MUP staff commander, the president of the provisional Executive Council of Kosovo, also the commander of the civil protection, Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Correct, sir. Many of the same people who attended the Joint Command meetings in 1998, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When those people were attending co-ordination and concerted action meetings, who was there, I just don't have that information. By and large though, those same men attended those meetings, at least, based on my second-hand information, such as I received from Djakovic and Colonel Djindjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. We'll move on to another topic now. You said in your testimony the other day that you have no reason to lie in your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You have no personal interest here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have a personal interest here because anything that I did during my time in Kosovo and Metohija and anything that I did for long years in the military security service is the truth that I know about Kosovo and Metohija which is also my PhD thesis, the genesis of the separatist movement. My uppermost motive in appearing here is to contribute to the establishment of truth. That is also my sole motive, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were a loyal member of the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are there any disloyal members of a regular army? Of course I was a loyal member.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, this Tribunal has prosecuted people you worked with and respected; correct? General Lazarevic, General Pavkovic. During the NATO bombing, you were on the same side as them, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the bombing, I was in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I mean, you were on the same side of that conflict. You, Pavkovic, Lazarevic, you fought on the same side together; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were on the side of our constitutional rights, and we were on the side of everything that that stood for. The protection of the country's constitution and territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And General Djordjevic was on that side too also? You were on the same side as General Djordjevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Kosovo is what you mean, I know that General Djordjevic was in Belgrade. I assume, however, given his elevated position, that he too would have been on the side of protecting the integrity of his country, which means the same side as me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, that was what I was asking you, sir, but I find it interesting that you are aware that general Djordjevic was in Belgrade. Did we not speak at the beginning of the cross-examination about your awareness of General Djordjevic's whereabouts? Do you recall we talked about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did talk about that, yes. Nevertheless, I'm talking about this as a whole. I'm talking about the gist of who was in Kosovo and Metohija all the time. And General Djordjevic certainly wasn't; he was chief of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, when I asked you questions about his whereabouts, you seemed to not really have very specific information about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, he was assistant minister in the public security sector, where on earth could he possibly have been? He was in the Ministry of the Interior, where else? You can't possibly be imagining he should have been elsewhere. He was assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying that because of an idea about the role of Mr. Djordjevic or because you had actual information about where he was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former, his role.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. Are you telling us that General Djordjevic was in Belgrade based on any actual information you have or based on your understanding that this is the Defence's theory of the case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm telling you that based on how the MUP functions, how the army functions, or indeed the federal institutions. In 1999, my knowledge indicates that General Djordjevic was not in Kosovo. On several occasions during the anti-terrorist operations, he was in Kosovo. I don't follow General Djordjevic's movements or whereabouts myself, but I did happen to have this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, the indictment in this case charges that the VJ and the MUP committed widespread war crimes in Kosovo in 1999. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt the well-founded nature of the indictment. I should assume that relevant evidence was gathered before the indictment was raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm just asking you if you know that that is basically what the indictment charges.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, that's when you yourself were in Kosovo, correct, with the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And part of your job was to detect and investigate such crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So the charges in this indictment are pertinent to you. In effect they mean that you either failed to detect massive crimes going on all around you or you're not telling us everything you know? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm telling you is this: Assessments made by official organs, my own superiors --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: No, that is not the question I'm asking you. I'm asking you if you understand the pertinence of the charges of the indictment to you? The charges in the indictment in effect mean or assert that you would have either been ignoring widespread crimes or are not actually telling us that. Do you understand that the indictment has that import, is pertinent to you in that way? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither is true in fact. I didn't know about --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you if you knew. I'm not asking you -- I'm asking you if you understand that because this indictment charges that there were widespread crimes, what that means for you is that you would either have not done your job or are not telling us what you actually know. That's what I'm asking you. Not if those are true, but if you understand that that's what the indictment -- how the indictment relates to you personally.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The allegations made in the indictment left a strong impression on me. The simple reason being I happen to believe that within the framework of my functional duty at the time, the duty I was discharging at the time, along with my subordinates, we knew quite well what the behaviour was of the army in Kosovo and Metohija in 1999. I do not dispute the possibility that some members of the army on a sporadic basis committed --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I have to stop you here. Maybe I'm not being clear enough. I am not asking you about your knowledge of crimes right now. I am asking you about your own personal reasons for not wanting this indictment to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. If the charges in this indictment are proven, then the only logical conclusion is that you yourself did not do your job, that you did not investigate crimes that were going on all around you, or that you aren't telling us what you know. Do you understand that that is the logical conclusion of the indictment being proven in this case? That is what I'm asking you, and I would like an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, you are cutting me off. I have every intention of answering all of your questions. I fully stand on the side of all of these crimes being punished. I will contribute in any way I can but only as far as I can stretch my knowledge. The nature of my job was precisely to prevent such things from happening. The other part of your question, I am here to give evidence about anything that I know. If you are asking me about something I don't know, that doesn't necessarily mean that I'm trying to conceal something that I actually do know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to a different question, sir. You have read the witness statement of Nike Peraj more than once; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time it was available to me, during my preparation for the Milutinovic trial, and then again during my preparation for my appearance here in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So you know that in his statement he says, and I will list a few things here, you know that he says, one, that you told him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Public or private?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: This is okay for public.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You know that he says that you told him in advance that there would be plans to expel the Albanian population from Djakovica and, two, that you called for retaliation for your relative's death; you know that he states that. Sir, I submit to you that you have a strong personal reason to undermine the testimony of Nike Peraj. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I'm entirely calm and my conscious is at ease. Far be it from me to react to some nebulous allegations being made, full of lies, nothing at all to do with the truth. I don't feel the need now or ever to take this out with Mr. Peraj in any way, simply because I have my wits about me and I'm fully conscious of my own actions. It is not my plan to look into the motives that drove Mr. Peraj to tell the lies that he did in his evidence and in his statement. My mind and my conscious is entirely at ease with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think you are answering my question. My question to you was: You have -- because of his allegations against you, which you know of, you have a strong personal reason to want to undermine his credibility before this Court, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've no reason to do anything. The only thing I have reason to do is to say that that is an untruth, Madam Prosecutor. I have no reason at all to busy myself with Nike Peraj's statement, which not only in relation to this particular statement, positively teems with lies. He was acting under the influence of the terrorist KLA, simply because he stayed on in Kosovo. And perhaps he was - I'm speaking hypothetically - simply ordered to say what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, you say you have no reason at all to busy yourself with his statement but you do agree that you've read it multiple times and have gone through paragraph by paragraph, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just have one more area to cover. We could either try to push through or -- it's not that much longer. Or we could -- you will see me again in the morning, hopefully not for very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness clearly can't finish today with re-examination, and we have, at the most, two minutes remaining. I think it would be preferable to delay until the morning, the completion of your questions. We adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 26th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
